title: DNS Terminology
summary: Gives current definitions for many terms used in DNS, which is specified in dozens of RFCs and whose terms have changed over the decades. It is Best Current Practice, and has been replaced by RFC 9499.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS has been described in dozens of RFCs since 1987, and the words they use have shifted over time. This RFC gathers the terms that DNS developers and operators use and gives each one a single agreed definition, grouped by topic.

questions: what does authoritative server mean in dns
what is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative server
what is an rrset in dns
what are the dnssec validation states
what does nodata mean in dns
subtitle: One document that fixes the meaning of the words DNS implementers, developers and operators use.

tldr.problem: The DNS is defined in dozens of RFCs written over decades, and the words used in them have drifted, so two experts can use the same term and mean different things.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects the terms in use, groups them by topic, and gives the consensus definition of each, quoting the earlier RFC when the consensus has not changed and writing a new stand-alone definition where it has.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8499 is a Best Current Practice, it obsoleted RFC 7719 and updated RFC 2308. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 9499.

today: RFC 8499 is a Best Current Practice published in January 2019. It obsoleted RFC 7719 and updated RFC 2308, and it has since been obsoleted by RFC 9499.

sections.title: Why a Terminology Document
sections.content:
The Domain Name System is a simple query-response protocol whose messages in both directions have the same format. The protocol and message format are defined in RFC 1034 and RFC 1035. Those RFCs defined some terms and later documents defined others, and some of the terms from RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 have somewhat different meanings now than they had in 1987.

The RFC collects a wide variety of DNS-related terms, organized loosely by topic. Some were precisely defined in earlier RFCs, some loosely, and some not at all. Other organizations define DNS-related terms their own way: the WHATWG defines domain in its own way, and the Root Server System Advisory Committee has a good lexicon of its own.

Most of the definitions represent the consensus of the DNS community, both protocol developers and operators. Some differ from earlier RFCs, and those differences are noted. Where the consensus definition is the same as the one in an RFC, that RFC is quoted. Where the consensus has changed somewhat, the RFC is mentioned but a new stand-alone definition is given, and Appendix A lists the definitions this document updates.

During the development of the document it became clear that some DNS-related terms are interpreted quite differently by different DNS experts, and that some terms defined in early DNS RFCs now have definitions that are generally agreed to but different from the original ones. That is why this document is a substantial revision to RFC 7719. There is no single consistent definition of the DNS: it can be considered some combination of a naming scheme for objects on the Internet, a distributed database of names and certain properties of those objects, an architecture providing distributed maintenance, resilience and loose coherency for that database, and the simple query-response protocol that implements the architecture. Section 2 defines global DNS and private DNS as a way to deal with those differing definitions.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS has been written about for decades and the words have drifted, so this RFC settles them. It says plainly where the agreed meaning matches an older RFC and where it has moved on.

sections.title: Names, Labels and the Global DNS
sections.content:
A naming system associates names with data, and the RFC lists the facets that help differentiate one naming system from another: the composition of names, their format, their administration, the types of data that can be associated with them, the types of metadata for names, the protocol for getting data from a name, and the context for resolving a name. The list is a small subset of the facets people have identified over time, chosen because it helps describe the DNS.

A domain name is an ordered list of one or more labels, and a label is an ordered list of zero or more octets that makes up a portion of a domain name. A fully-qualified domain name includes every label, including the zero-length label of the root, and is written with a terminating dot, for example www.example.net. Because every name eventually shares the common root, names are often written relative to the root, such as www.example.net, and are still called fully qualified, and in this document names are often written that way.

The global DNS is described using the same set of facets. A name in the global DNS has one or more labels, each between 0 and 63 octets long, and a domain name has a maximum total length of 255 octets in the wire format, with the root counting as one octet. Names have three formats: the wire format, a list of labels each preceded by a length octet; the presentation format, the same labels written as ASCII with a dot between each, so that a fully-qualified name is shown as example.tld.; and the common display format, which is the presentation format with the trailing root dot left off, so example.tld.

Private DNS is the name space for names that use the DNS protocol but do not rely on the global DNS root zone, or that are not generally available on the Internet. A system can use the global DNS and one or more private DNS systems at the same time, as in split DNS. Multicast DNS performs DNS-like operations on the local link in the absence of any conventional unicast DNS server; it uses a compatible wire format but is strictly speaking a different protocol, and its names are not intended to be looked up in the DNS.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain name is a list of labels read from the top level downwards, and a label is a piece of that list. The same name has three written forms: the form on the wire, the form with a trailing dot, and the form people write in free text.

sections.title: Response Codes and Negative Answers
sections.content:
Some of the response codes defined in RFC 1035 have acquired their own shorthand names. All of the codes are listed in the IANA registry, although that list uses mixed-case capitalization while most documents use all caps.

NOERROR appears as no error condition. FORMERR appears as format error, the name server was unable to interpret the query. SERVFAIL appears as server failure, the name server was unable to process the query because of a problem with the name server. NXDOMAIN appears as name error, meaning the domain name referenced in the query does not exist; RFC 2308 established NXDOMAIN as a synonym for Name Error. NOTIMP appears as not implemented, the name server does not support the requested kind of query. REFUSED appears as refused, the name server refuses to perform the specified operation for policy reasons, for example because it does not wish to provide the information to a particular requester or does not wish to perform a particular operation such as a zone transfer.

NODATA is described as a pseudo code, indicating that the name is valid for the given class but there are no records of the given type. It has to be inferred from the answer: the code is set to NOERROR and the answer section holds nothing relevant, while the authority section contains an SOA record or there are no NS records there. Referrals have a similar format, and RFC 2308 explains how to tell them apart. The term NXRRSET is sometimes used as a synonym for NODATA, but the RFC calls that a mistake, since NXRRSET is a specific error code defined in RFC 2136. A negative response is one that indicates that a particular RRset does not exist, or whose response code indicates that the name server cannot answer.
sections.plainLanguage: The last four bits of a DNS reply carry a status code. The important ones are NXDOMAIN, which says the name does not exist, and NODATA, which says the name exists but has no records of the type you asked for.

sections.title: Resolvers, Recursion and Authoritative Servers
sections.content:
A resolver is a program that extracts information from name servers in response to client requests: it performs queries for a name, type and class and receives responses, and that logical function is called resolution. There is no formal definition of DNS server, and RFCs generally assume an Internet server that listens for queries and sends responses using the DNS protocol. The terms DNS server and name server require context, because authoritative servers and recursive resolvers are often called by both names even though they serve different roles, though they may be part of the same software package.

An authoritative server is a server that knows the content of a DNS zone from local knowledge, and can therefore answer queries about that zone without querying other servers. It is named in the NS record of a zone and sets the AA flag in the response header to 1. It also provides referrals, usually to child zones delegated from it; those referrals have the AA bit set to 0 and carry referral data in the authority section and, if needed, the additional section. An authoritative-only server serves authoritative data and ignores requests for recursion.

A stub resolver is a resolver that cannot perform all resolution itself and depends on a recursive resolver to do the actual work. A recursive resolver is a resolver that acts in recursive mode: it answers queries either from a local cache or by sending queries to other servers to get the final answer, and in that mode it returns either an error or the answer, but never referrals. A resolver that works in iterative mode instead responds with a referral to another server and lets the client pursue the query. A recursive query is one with the RD bit set to 1 in the header, and a client can check that recursive mode was used by looking for both RA and RD set in the reply. An iterative resolver repeatedly makes non-recursive queries and follows referrals and aliases.

A referral is a response in which a server signals that it is not completely authoritative for an answer and gives the querying resolver another place to send the query. A downward referral, sometimes called a delegation response, is where the server is authoritative for part of the name; the authority section holds the NS RRset of the referred-to zone cut, and the AA bit is clear. An upward referral, sometimes called a root referral, is where the server is not authoritative for any part of the name; the referred-to zone is usually the root, this kind of referral is not required for resolution, and some people regard it as a sign of a misconfiguration.
sections.plainLanguage: An authoritative server holds the real data for a zone and answers for it. A recursive resolver does the legwork on behalf of a client and returns the answer or an error. A referral is the instruction to go and ask somebody else.

sections.title: Zones, Delegations and Zone Cuts
sections.content:
Authoritative information is organized into units called zones, and these zones can be automatically distributed to the name servers that provide redundant service for the data in a zone. A zone cut is the delimitation point between two zones where the origin of one zone is the child of the other; each zone cut separates a child zone from a parent zone. Delegation is the process by which a separate zone is created in the name space beneath the apex of a given domain, and it happens when an NS RRset is added in the parent zone for the child origin. The term is also used as a noun for the new zone that results.

The origin is the domain name that appears at the top of a zone, just below the cut that separates the zone from its parent, and the name of the zone is the same as the name of the domain at the zone's origin; the second use of the word is the domain name within which a relative name appears in zone files, as in $ORIGIN. The apex is the point in the tree at which an owner of an SOA and the corresponding authoritative NS RRset sits, also called the zone apex.

A lame delegation exists when a name server is delegated responsibility for providing name service for a zone but is not performing name service for that zone, usually because it is not set up as a primary or secondary for it. Queries then go to servers that know nothing about the domain. Glue records are address records for name servers that are not part of the authoritative data of the zone, and they are needed only when the name server's own name lies below the cut.

Section 8 of the RFC defines wildcards, including the asterisk label, the closest encloser and the source of synthesis. Section 9 defines the registration model: the registry, which is whoever decides what data goes into a zone; the registrant, on whose behalf a name is registered; the registrar, a service provider that acts as a go-between; the Extensible Provisioning Protocol used to exchange registration information between registries and registrars; and WHOIS, often used for querying registry databases.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS is cut into zones, each served by its own servers. Where one zone hands part of its name space to another, that boundary is a zone cut, and the servers named there are expected to answer for it.

sections.title: The Four DNSSEC States
sections.content:
Section 11 of the RFC records the four states a validating resolver can determine for a response, as defined in RFC 4033 and RFC 4035. Secure means the resolver has a trust anchor, has a chain of trust, and can verify all the signatures in the response. Insecure means the resolver has a trust anchor and a chain of trust, and at some delegation point there is signed proof that no DS record exists, which indicates that subsequent branches in the tree are provably insecure. Bogus means the resolver has a trust anchor and a secure delegation saying the subsidiary data is signed, but the response fails to validate, for example through missing signatures, expired signatures, signatures with unsupported algorithms, or data missing that the relevant NSEC record says should be present. Indeterminate means there is no trust anchor indicating that the specific portion of the tree is secure, which is the default operation mode.

The definitions of these states in RFC 4033 and RFC 4035 differ slightly, and this document makes no effort to reconcile them and takes no position on whether they need to be. The security considerations section itself is short: these definitions do not change any security considerations for the DNS. The document also has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: When a resolver checks signatures, it ends up in one of four situations: the data checks out, the data is provably not signed, the data should have been signed but does not validate, or the resolver cannot tell. The names for those four are secure, insecure, bogus and indeterminate.

items.label: Format error
items.desc: The name server was unable to interpret the query.

items.label: Server failure
items.desc: The name server was unable to process the query because of a problem with itself.

items.label: Name error
items.desc: The domain name referenced in the query does not exist.

items.label: Not implemented
items.desc: The name server does not support the requested kind of query.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: The name server refuses to perform the operation for policy reasons.

items.label: No data
items.desc: A pseudo code: the name is valid, but there are no records of the given type.

A resolver that answers queries from a local cache or by querying other servers itself
On a query it cannot answer

Looks up the answer itself and returns the answer or an error, but never a referral
Named in the NS record of a zone and sets the AA flag to 1

viz.caption: THE FOUR STATES OF A VALIDATING RESOLVER

items.title: Secure
items.text: The resolver has a trust anchor, a chain of trust, and can verify all the signatures.

items.title: Insecure
items.text: Signed proof shows that no DS record exists, so later branches are provably insecure.

items.title: Bogus
items.text: The data should have been signed, but the response fails to validate.

items.title: Indeterminate
items.text: No trust anchor indicates that this part of the tree is secure.
